view: Gabriel told Joseph he would leave prison the next day. Joseph asked about Jacob, whose grief had blinded him, and was told that Jacob's reward equaled that of one hundred martyrs.
The survivor of the two prisoners was the king's cupbearer or wine server, the one who dreamed of pressing wine; the other prisoner was executed.

The cupbearer remembered Joseph after hearing the king and his court struggle with the dream. He recalled Joseph's accurate interpretations of his and the baker's dreams and Joseph's request to be mentioned to the king.
note: Some reports name the cupbearer Nabū; some specify that the earlier interpretations made him trust Joseph's knowledge.

view: The cupbearer's remembering Joseph and his earlier request supports the account that the cupbearer, rather than Joseph, forgot in the preceding story.
note: Ibn ʿAṭiyya leaves the earlier question open.

view: The verb can mean simply 'remembered and told' or 'mentioned'; its reflexive form does not by itself establish an earlier lapse of memory, just as other reflexive forms can equal simpler verbs.
note: This bears on whether Joseph or the cupbearer forgot earlier.

view: The expressions used for remembering are synonymous.

The common form ادّكر derives from an underlying اذتكر or اذْتكر: the infixed tāʾ changes to dāl and the adjacent dhāl assimilates, yielding doubled dāl. The substitution accommodates voicing and articulation and is described as the more eloquent form.
note: Al-Akhfash says ṭāʾ is avoided because of emphasis, and compares the consonant behavior of أن يصلحا and يصطلحا at 4:128.

view: An alternative morphological analysis replaces the infixed tāʾ with dhāl before assimilation, producing a form with doubled dhāl.

The common reading has doubled dāl; al-Ḥasan reads a form with dhāl instead, traced to تذكّر or an alternative assimilation. Sources call the dāl form more eloquent, while acknowledging the dhāl form.
note: The notes describe al-Ḥasan's form variously as وذكر, واذكر, or واَدّكر with dhāl.

view: Mujāhid read the verb with a jussive ending and a softened consonant.
The clause 'and remembered' is most likely circumstantial, referring to the survivor, though it can also be coordinated with 'survived.'
The verb can be understood as 'he sought to remember.'
Discussion of وادّكر is linked to the related form مدّكر in Sūrat al-Qamar; a report says the Prophet recited that related form in Q 54:15.
أمّة here means a span, long period, age, or years that passed after the cupbearer's release; the length is unspecified in this explanation.
note: Some reports say only God knows the interval; others specify years.

view: The interval after the cupbearer's release was seven years.
note: The Study Quran connects the interval with Joseph's imprisonment in 12:42.

view: The interval after Joseph and the cupbearer separated was four years.
The Torah gives the interval of forgetfulness as two years.
The time sense of أمّة is explained through its sense of a collected group: many days and hours form a span, or a whole generation passes during it. A generation itself can be an ummah.
note: Ibn Durustawayh says the time sense requires an omitted word such as 'period'; Ibn ʿĀshūr relates the generation sense to one reading of Q 3:110.

view: أمّة can mean a group united in purpose or a large community; it has singular form and collective meaning, and each animal species can be called a community.
A hadith says that if dogs were not a community among communities, the Prophet would have ordered them killed.
note: Cited in support of the collective sense of أمّة.

view: Calling the interval an أمّة emphasizes how long the cupbearer forgot Joseph.

A noncanonical reading has a light, open form such as بعد أمه or بعد أمة instead of doubled-mīm أُمّة, giving the sense 'after forgetfulness.' Reports attribute forms of it to Ibn ʿAbbās, Ibn ʿUmar, ʿIkrima, al-Ḍaḥḥāk, Qatāda, Zayd ibn ʿAlī, and others.
note: Transmissions differ over some readers and over final hāʾ or tāʾ.

view: The light form أمه means forgetfulness, from أمه / أمه يأمه, 'to forget'; Arabic poetry using أمِهَ supports the sense.
note: This explains remembering after forgetting, rather than merely after a span of time.

view: Mujāhid and others read a light form with still mīm as a verbal noun meaning forgetfulness; some describe the still and moving mīm as dialect forms.

The still-mīm form for 'forgetfulness' is disputed: al-Zajjāj and al-Zamakhsharī reject it, while Abū al-Haytham and later commentators defend it as an attested reading; Abū al-Haytham instead rejects the moving-mīm form.
note: The disagreement turns on which vowel pattern is a valid verbal noun of forgetting.

view: Al-Ḥasan reads the phrase as 'after a people' or 'after a community had passed.'
Al-Ashhab al-ʿUqaylī reads إمة or عِمّة with an initial kasra, taking it to mean a blessing, favor, or prosperous condition; a line of ʿAdī ibn Zayd is cited for that sense.
Under the 'blessing' reading, the favor is the cupbearer's survival, freedom from execution and prison, and the king's kindness to him.
Under the 'blessing' reading, the favor is God's bringing Joseph close to release and honor.
note: Al-Ālūsī calls this explanation far-fetched.

view: The phrase 'after a time' interrupts the speech introduction and its quoted content; it may be circumstantial with an understood قد, while analysis as part of the relative clause is rejected because the later remembering supplies new information.
The preposition بعد is governed by ادّكر.
The cupbearer delayed telling the king about Joseph because mentioning him might recall the offense that had sent the cupbearer to prison.
note: These notes set this against an explanation by forgetfulness.

view: The cupbearer's forgetting, and Joseph's continued imprisonment, occurred by God's decree; one account says both Joseph and the cupbearer forgot.
note: Competing accounts attribute the delay to fear of mentioning the former offense.

view: The cupbearer offers to report the king's dream interpretation by consulting Joseph, the person who knows it, rather than from his own knowledge.
note: Some notes add that he cited Joseph's earlier accurate interpretations.

view: By beginning with 'I' and presenting himself as the subject, the cupbearer surprises the king and lends force to his claim that he can resolve a dream that baffled the court.
The cupbearer figuratively says that he himself will inform them because he will cause the interpretation to reach them.
The cupbearer leaves Joseph unnamed so that news of a prisoner's skill will surprise the court and carry more force.

The cupbearer cautiously offers to return with Joseph's interpretation so people will recognize Joseph's learning; his wording allows for the possibility of failure after the other interpreters failed.
The clause 'I will inform you' is the quotation governed by 'he said.'
One canonical recitation uses a short final vowel in أنا; another lengthens its final ā with madd.

Al-Ḥasan reads 'I will bring you its interpretation' (أنا آتيكم) instead of 'I will inform you'; Ubayy's codex also transmits this form. Al-Zajjāj objects that it differs from the written consonantal text.
note: The reciter asks whether Joseph was their prophet or the cupbearer truly informed them; al-Ḥasan is also said to avoid claiming the interpretation as his own.

view: The standard أنبّئكم means 'I will tell you' when asked.
The plural 'you' addresses the king and the officials around him, who manage his affairs; the later 'I shall return to the people' is cited in support.
The plural address can be an honorific to the king alone, whose attendants share his command.
note: The competing view takes the plural as addressed to the king and his court.

view: The cupbearer asks the king or court to permit and send him to Joseph in prison to ask for the dream's interpretation.
note: One report has him kneel before the king and ask to visit a knowledgeable man.

view: The narrative omits the court's permission, the cupbearer's dispatch and journey to Joseph, and his arrival at the prison.
Yaʿqūb keeps the first-person yāʾ in 'send me' both in connected recitation and at pause; another recitation elides it at pause.
A report of Ubayy's codex explicitly includes فأرسلون, understood as asking to be sent to Joseph for the interpretation.
Reports place Joseph's prison outside the king's city, explaining why the cupbearer needed to be sent out to him.
note: Competing reports place the prison within the city; al-Ālūsī leaves its actual location to God.

view: Other reports place Joseph's prison inside the king's city.
note: Competes with the reports that it was outside the city.

view: People in Ibn ʿAṭiyya's day identified Joseph's prison beside the Nile, eight miles from Fusṭāṭ.
The cupbearer's confidence that Joseph was still in prison suggests a private prison whose inmates' release or death would have become known at court.
Al-Ḥasan reports Joseph entered the well at seventeen, spent eighty years in servitude, prison, and kingship, and lived twenty-three years after reunion with his family.
Confused dreams and passing inner thoughts are disregarded, whereas a true vision can be interpreted and investigated.
note: This relates the cupbearer's offer to the courtiers' preceding judgment of the king's dream.

view: The officials call the king's vision a jumble of dreams and say they cannot interpret such mixed dreams.
note: This precedes the cupbearer's offer.

view: The officials' response can instead mean that they cannot interpret dreams generally, or that they can interpret only true dreams.
note: Alternative understandings of their preceding statement.

view: Al-Qummī narrates the king's dream of seven fat cows consumed by lean cows and green and dry ears, the cupbearer's later remembrance, and Joseph's interpretation of seven plentiful years, seven famine years, and then rain.
Joseph hears the king's dream and explains it without reproaching the cupbearer for forgetting him or first demanding release.
The cupbearer hoped to return with Joseph's interpretation either to explain the dream or to show Joseph's knowledge and secure his release.
The Qur'anic account of Joseph illustrates God's direction of human affairs: people may dislike what benefits them and favor what harms them, as Q 2:216 says.
note: The note contrasts this theme with Genesis' account.

view: Yughāth in the neighboring interpretation may derive from rescue and relief or from rain; an Arab woman's request for rain illustrates the latter sense.
Ṣiddīq is an intensive form meaning very truthful or strongly affirming truth; the cupbearer uses it for Joseph after long acquaintance and the accuracy of his earlier dream interpretations.
In the related grammatical discussion, يصطلحا is preferred to أن يصلحا; ṣād does not assimilate into tāʾ because of voicing and emphasis, so tāʾ changes instead.
note: An analogy for the assimilation discussed under وادّكر.
